summary: SIP servers can become overloaded, and the basic 503 response does not protect them well. This document defines the behavior of SIP servers involved in overload control and specifies a loss-based scheme in which servers tell upstream senders how much traffic to reduce.

eli5.summary: When a restaurant is too full, the host tells arriving groups to wait. This RFC gives phone-call servers a way to tell others to send fewer requests so they do not get swamped.

questions: how do sip servers handle overload
what does the oc parameter do in sip
subtitle: How a SIP server that is drowning in requests tells its neighbours to send fewer, using four new Via header parameters.

tldr.problem: When a SIP server receives more messages than it can process, throughput drops and retransmissions can lead to congestion collapse. The 503 (Service Unavailable) response cannot prevent this and may make it worse by shifting traffic back and forth between servers.
tldr.mechanism: The sender adds oc and oc-algo parameters to its Via header. The overloaded server answers with a value in oc (for the loss-based scheme, a percentage of requests to cut), plus oc-validity and oc-seq, and the sender reduces its traffic accordingly.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7339 is a Proposed Standard. The loss-based scheme is mandatory to implement, and other schemes can be added through the oc-algo list.

today: RFC 7339 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves other schemes, such as a rate-based one, to separate documents.

sections.title: The Overload Problem
sections.content:
A SIP server is overloaded when it does not have enough resources, such as CPU, memory, input/output or disk, to process all the messages it receives. During overload the throughput of a whole network of SIP servers can degrade, and retransmissions of dropped messages can overwhelm the network. The RFC calls this congestion collapse.

SIP already has a limited tool, the 503 (Service Unavailable) response. The RFC says it cannot prevent overload or congestion collapse and may even make things worse by making traffic oscillate between servers. RFC 7339 defines a protocol for servers to tell clients how much to cut back, so that useful throughput stays up.

The scope is narrow: only failures caused by resource constraints. A gateway that has run out of trunks but can still process SIP messages should reject with 488, and a registrar that lost its database should reject with 500. Overload control does not apply to those cases. The background and requirements are in RFC 5390.
sections.eli5: If too many people knock on a shop door at once, nobody gets served. The shop needs a way to say 'please send fewer people', not just slam the door.

sections.title: The Four Via Parameters
sections.content:
Overload control is hop by hop, so the RFC puts its signals in the Via header, which only the adjacent neighbours see. Four parameters are defined:

  • oc: the client adds it, with no value, to the topmost Via of every request to show support. The server fills in a value in the response. For the loss-based scheme the value is the percentage reduction wanted.
  • oc-algo: the client lists the classes of algorithm it supports, with loss always included. The server picks one and returns it as the only value.
  • oc-validity: set by the server, in milliseconds, for how long the reduction applies. The default is 500. A value of 0 means the server wants to stop overload control.
  • oc-seq: set by the server, an increasing number (a timestamp works) so the client can tell newer feedback from stale or out-of-order responses.

Clients MUST NOT put oc-validity or oc-seq in requests.
sections.eli5: It is like a note stuck on the reply: how much to slow down, how long that lasts, and a number so you know which note is the newest.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Behave
sections.content:
On first contact the client sends oc and oc-algo. A server that is not overloaded picks an algorithm and answers with oc=0, optionally with oc-validity=0. If it is overloaded it sends a real value. A server that does not support the extension leaves the parameters unchanged, which tells the client it does not take part.

The client stores the values per server address and port. A response with a larger oc-seq replaces the stored values and restarts the validity timer. Overload control ends when the validity period runs out or when the server sends oc-validity=0. The client MUST NOT send more requests than the current values allow, and it SHOULD strip the parameters from lower Via headers so they cannot travel upstream.

To cut traffic the client can send requests to another, healthy destination, buffer them, or reject them with 503 without a Retry-After header. It SHOULD follow local priority policy, such as message type, the Resource-Priority header (RFC 4412) and emergency calls.

Once a server has chosen an algorithm for a client it SHOULD NOT change it for at least 3600 seconds. Clients that keep timing out MUST stop sending and probe conservatively, for example with exponential back-off. A server that is throttling MUST reject some requests from non-participating clients with 503, so that supporting clients get no disadvantage.
sections.eli5: The busy server says how much to slow down and for how long. The sender follows that note, and when the time is up or the server says all clear, goes back to normal speed.

sections.title: The Loss-Based Scheme
sections.content:
In the loss-based scheme (token loss) the server asks the client to reduce the requests it would normally forward by a percentage. The oc value MUST be in the range 0 to 100. A value of 10 means 10 percent of all requests, dialogue-forming and in-dialogue, are subject to reduction.

Any algorithm that produces the requested reduction is acceptable, but the RFC gives a default. The client splits requests into category 1 (candidates for reduction) and category 2 (protected unless category 1 is exhausted). If oc=10 and 40 percent of requests are in category 1, then 10 / 40 * 100 = 25 percent of category 1 is discarded. The client draws a random number between 1 and 100 for each category 1 request and does not forward it when the number is less than or equal to the converted value. The traffic mix is re-sampled periodically, for example every 5 to 10 seconds.
sections.eli5: If the server asks you to cut 10 out of every 100 letters, you pick the less important ones at random to hold back and keep the important ones.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
Client P1 sends an INVITE to server P2 with oc and oc-algo="loss,A". P2 supports the scheme, so its 100 Trying returns oc=0, oc-algo="loss" and oc-validity=0: it supports overload control but is not asking for any reduction.

Later P2 becomes overloaded, and a 180 Ringing carries oc=20 and oc-validity=500 with an oc-seq value, asking P1 for a 20 percent cut for 0.5 seconds. When the overload eases, a 183 Queued response carries oc=0 and oc-validity=0 with a higher oc-seq, and P1 may send everything again.
sections.eli5: First the server says 'all fine'. Then it says 'slow down by a fifth for half a second'. Finally it says 'back to normal'.

sections.title: Design Choices
sections.content:
The RFC compares two ways to carry overload feedback. A Via parameter adds almost no overhead, needs no extra messages, reaches only senders that are currently active, and updates as often as responses flow. A SIP event package would let a receiver notify inactive senders, but it needs subscriptions with every neighbour, adds NOTIFY traffic that itself needs priority handling, and forces each proxy to act as a user agent.

On compatibility, hop-by-hop control works between any two adjacent supporting servers. Because non-supporting clients would otherwise benefit from the throttling of others, servers must reject some of their requests too. The RFC also says its reactive mechanism does not discriminate by user identity and that pro-active load filters from RFC 7200 may be used alongside, with local policy deciding precedence.
sections.eli5: Putting the note on the reply you are already sending is cheaper than mailing a separate letter to everyone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The feedback itself can be abused. An attacker who can modify traffic on a link can forge an overload indication, so that the sender stops sending to the victim, or can strip genuine oc markings so that a server stays flooded. The RFC says TLS combined with BCP 38 (RFC 2827) best mitigates these attacks.

Other threats are an attacker injecting feedback through a proxy that does not support the extension, a malicious entity that claims support but never reduces traffic (servers should monitor clients and treat non-conforming ones as non-supporting), and a distributed denial-of-service attack synchronized with a long oc-validity interval. Defences against the last one are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Someone could fake a 'we are full' sign to keep customers away, so the sign needs to come from a trusted source.

messages.label: INVITE oc; oc-algo="loss,A"
messages.note: P1 signals support and lists its algorithms.

items.label: Reduction level
items.desc: Added empty by the client; the server sets the value (a percentage for the loss scheme).

items.label: Algorithm class
items.desc: Client lists supported classes, always including loss; server returns the one chosen.

items.label: Validity in ms
items.desc: Server only. Default 500; 0 ends overload control.

items.label: Sequence number
items.desc: Server only. Increasing, so stale feedback can be recognised.
